title: Loading States
description: Design helpful loading experiences with loading.tsx, Suspense fallbacks, and skeleton loaders that keep users informed while data loads.

data.text: A good loading state does more than show a spinner. It communicates what is happening, sets expectations, and keeps the user engaged. Next.js makes it easy to add loading states at the route level with loading.tsx and at the component level with React Suspense.

Loading states are especially important when data takes more than a few hundred milliseconds to load. Without clear feedback, users may think the application is broken or try to click buttons multiple times.

Create a loading.tsx file in any route segment to show a loading UI while Server Components in that segment fetch data. Next.js automatically wraps the segment in a Suspense boundary and displays the loading file while waiting. The loading file is a Client Component by default, so you can use interactivity if needed.

data.title: Skeleton loading UI
data.content: A skeleton loading UI that mimics the shape of the actual content.

data.text: Skeleton loaders are placeholders that resemble the final layout. They reduce perceived wait time because users can preview the page structure before content arrives. Use Tailwind's animate-pulse class to create a subtle shimmer effect that indicates content is loading.

items: Match the shape and size of the final content as closely as possible
Use subtle animations like pulse or shimmer to show activity
Avoid large blank areas that make the page feel broken
Keep skeleton screens simple and fast to render

data.text: Inside Server Components, wrap slow sections in Suspense boundaries with a fallback prop. The fallback can be a spinner, a skeleton, or a minimal placeholder. Each boundary controls its own loading state, so different sections can appear independently.

data.content: Multiple Suspense boundaries in a dashboard, each with its own skeleton fallback.

items: Show loading states for any fetch expected to take longer than 200 milliseconds
Use skeletons for known content shapes and spinners for unknown shapes
Do not disable buttons without indicating why — add a loading state
Avoid flashing loading states for fast fetches under 200 milliseconds
Combine route loading files with nested Suspense for progressive dashboards

data.title: Pro Tip
data.text: If a fetch consistently finishes in under 200 milliseconds, skip the loading state and let the content appear instantly. Frequent flickering between skeleton and content feels worse than a small initial delay.

data.title: Summary
points: Loading states keep users informed and reduce perceived wait time.
Use loading.tsx for route-level loading and Suspense fallbacks for component-level control.
Skeleton loaders mirror the final layout for a smoother experience.
Design loading states to feel like part of the page, not interruptions.
Skip loading states for fast fetches under 200 milliseconds to avoid flicker.
